## February 29, 1960

You entered the world on one of the rarest days in the calendar — a date that exists only once every four years. In 66 years of life, you have had exactly sixteen actual February 29 birthdays. Your next one arrives in 2028. This is not a quirk; it is the opening note of a life defined by a slightly tilted relationship to ordinary time.

---

**The ground shook that day — literally.** On February 29, 1960, a shallow earthquake struck the Moroccan city of Agadir while most of its residents slept. In roughly fifteen seconds, between 12,000 and 15,000 people died and a modern city was erased. It was one of the deadliest earthquakes of the twentieth century. The world you arrived in that morning was already being jolted out of its postwar assumptions.

**Twenty-eight days before your birth**, four Black college students — Franklin McCain, Ezell Blair Jr., Joseph McNeil, and David Richmond — sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave. By the day you were born, their action had ignited sit-ins in dozens of cities across the South. The civil rights movement had been building for years, but February 1960 was the moment it became impossible to dismiss as regional or marginal. The country into which you drew your first breath was in the middle of deciding what kind of country it intended to be.

**Three days earlier**, British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan had stood before the South African parliament and delivered what became known as the "Wind of Change" speech — acknowledging, from within the heart of the apartheid system, that African nationalism was a force no colonial power could stop. In 1960 alone, seventeen African nations would gain independence. The map of the world was being redrawn in real time around your cradle.

**Eisenhower was in the White House**, but the election year had already begun. A young senator from Massachusetts named John F. Kennedy was running hard for the Democratic nomination. By November — when you were eight months old — he would win the presidency by the narrowest margin in modern American history, and the country would enter a decade it could not yet imagine.

**The world your parents knew was ending in other ways too.** Just months after your birth, in May 1960, the FDA would approve the first oral contraceptive. This was not merely a medical approval; it was one of the most consequential social disruptions of the century, and it would reshape the world you grew up in.

---

**What the lifetime looks like from here:**

You were nine when humans walked on the Moon — old enough to understand what had happened, young enough to absorb it as a normal fact about what people can do. You were twenty-nine when the Berlin Wall fell and the Cold War that had been the permanent backdrop of your entire life simply stopped. You were forty-one on September 11, 2001. You watched the internet go from novelty to nervous system. You have seen the rise of the personal computer, the smartphone, and now artificial intelligence, each one restructuring daily life more thoroughly than the last.

You entered a world of typewriters and rotary phones and three television channels, a world where photographs took two weeks to develop and long-distance phone calls were rationed like luxuries. The world you inhabit in 2026 is not an updated version of that world; it is a fundamentally different civilization.

---

You were born on the rarest day, in the hinge year of a century. The Agadir earthquake, the Greensboro sit-ins, the Wind of Change, the dawn of Kennedy's America — these were not merely the backdrop of your arrival. They were the first hours of the world you would help make.
